articles.title: Community efforts revive historic Lodge Mill after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton, a historic site dating back to 1850, is seeing a revival thanks to community support following a fire that left it in ruins.
articles.content_html:
Lodge Mill, one of the oldest mills in Middleton, is undergoing a revival after a devastating fire left the historic structure nearly destroyed. The fire, which occurred earlier this year, resulted in the loss of significant parts of the mill, including a children's dance studio and an ice cream parlour. Fortunately, no injuries were reported during the incident.

The mill, which dates back to around 1850, was deemed uninsurable following the fire, complicating efforts for its restoration. However, local residents and volunteers have rallied together to support the rebuilding efforts. A GoFundMe page was established, raising over £7,000 to aid in the restoration process, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving this historic landmark.

Martin and Paula, who were actively working on renovating the three floors above Lodge Mill prior to the fire, are now at the forefront of the recovery efforts. Thanks to the dedication of volunteers, life is returning to Lodge Mill, with plans to restore it to its former glory.

The revival of Lodge Mill is significant not only for its historical value but also for the community spirit it embodies. As restoration efforts continue, the mill is set to become a focal point for local activities once again, highlighting the importance of community involvement in preserving local heritage.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The potential return of Lodge Mill | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The potential return of Lodge Mill George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 24, 2026 | 2 hours ago Print Community effort to clear up rubble at Lodge Mill in Middleton Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill. Rubble has been moved from the old Engine Room and more than 120 pallets of full bricks, Yorkshire Stone and specialty bricks have been picked up by hand and stacked. The annual duck race was held at the site in May, the ice cream shop has reopened and there are upcoming events for Halloween and Christmas. There is a long-term vision to bring the mill back into proper use again, with businesses on the ground floor and new flats above. But before that can happen, the site needs to be cleared. One keen volunteer is Dawn Alker, she visited The Ice Cream Shop at Lodge around eight years ago. She has returned many times since, but most recently as a volunteer. She said: “I went there for ice cream about seven or eight years ago and fell in love with the place. When it burnt down they asked for volunteers to clean it up. “Everyone goes down and chips in and does what they can on the day. “I used to be a manager in the NHS and now I am making a monster for Halloween in a burnt down mill. “It’s really nice to be working collectively. It’s turned into a community support project in a way. “I have mental health issues and I had stopped going outside and stayed inside too much. I started helping, selfishly, because I wanted the ice cream place back open again. “My mental health started to improve as I got moving more and others have said the same. “In terms of the project we have got to clear the site because it was bulldozed. Then the end goal is to rebuild it. “Then we want small businesses with flats over the top of them. That is just a vision at the moment. “It is going to  be a long project but it is going to be brilliant.” Dawn went on to say that the managers of Lodge Mill, Martin and Paula, have already instructed architects and looked at the structural integrity of the remaining walls at the mill. The business owners are hoping to submit planning proposals to the council in the coming months. articles.title: Nine-year-old guitar virtuoso Adrian Abraham from Middleton on verge of world record
articles.excerpt: Adrian Abraham, a nine-year-old from Middleton, is set to make his mark in the music world as he approaches a potential world record for his guitar skills, inspired by his father and a passion for heavy metal.
articles.content_html:
Adrian Abraham, a nine-year-old guitar virtuoso from Middleton, is on the verge of setting a world record for his exceptional guitar skills. Having started his musical journey approximately two years ago, Adrian has rapidly developed his talent, showcasing his abilities through performances shared on his Instagram account.

Initially picking up an acoustic guitar, Adrian soon transitioned to electric guitar, where he found his passion for heavy metal music. Inspired by his father, who introduced him to the instrument, Adrian has dedicated himself to mastering various genres, although heavy metal remains his favourite.

As he prepares for his first live performance, Adrian aims to inspire others to take up an instrument, demonstrating that dedication and passion can lead to remarkable achievements at a young age. His journey reflects not only his personal growth but also the potential for young musicians to make an impact in the music industry.

Adrian's story is a testament to the power of inspiration and hard work, and as he approaches this potential world record, the local community is eager to support his musical aspirations.

Adrian Abraham, from Middleton, only started playing the guitar about two years ago. Later this month, he is taking the Trinity College London Grade 8 Rock & Pop electric guitar examination — and could win a Guinness World Record in the process. Adrian loves heavy metal and picked up the guitar after hearing his father, Abraham Joseph, play the acoustic guitar. His favourite band is Iron Maiden and his favourite song to play is Eruption, by Van Halen. His Instagram page features dozens of videos chronicling his journey, including performances of hits by Metallica, Guns ‘n’ Roses, Queen, Deep Purple, Slipknot and System of a Down. The youngster said: “I saw my dad playing the guitar and I thought it really sounded cool, and then I wanted to give it a try. Adrian prepares for his first live performance. Image: adrian_jaams “So then I gave it a shot and I started going through acoustic at first and eventually went to electric.” Abraham added: “I used to play acoustic guitar and he used to sit down and listen. One day he told me he wanted to just hold the guitar to get the feel of it. “He took the guitar and he held a perfect cord. That’s the time I realised the guitar is the instrument for him. “His first guitar was a classic acoustic guitar which he played for about three months before it wasn’t enough for him and we had to upgrade to an electric. He is really progressing well. “I’ve been in choirs and I picked up the acoustic guitar when I was in college. It was just for fun and then I left it, but then when Adrian was born, I had this overwhelming feeling I should play something to him which would sound good. Music brings the out a real person. “But then he reached a point where he discovering grade eight. I can only teach him as much as basics of the guitar but the further grades, he picked it up himself.” With the help of a tutor, Adrian could now become the youngest person to pass the Grade 8 rock and pop guitar exam, setting a world record. He said: “I feel very excited and happy that I could be beating a world record, and I’m very happy that I got this far. If I beat it, I’m gonna be so overjoyed!” READ MORE: New drive to open car wash in town Adrian has been given a Marshall amplifier and Solar guitar by the manufacturers. Image: adrian_jaams While Adrian has to showcase a range of techniques for the exam, playing his favourite song is already a challenge for guitarists. With more than 200 beats per minute, it requires a tapping technique, using fingers from each hand, instead of picking or plucking. Adrian said: “My favourite song would be Eruption from Van Halen, and since I just really like the tapping pod and it just really gets me. It is the most-iconic tapping song in the world and it just sounds absolutely great.” The youngster’s ability has earned global attention, including endorsements from legendary music industry brands Marshall Amplifiers and Solar Guitars, which have supplied him with equipment to help his music journey. Following his exams, the natural outlet for Adrian’s talent would be playing in a band. Abraham said: “When people hear Adrian, a lot of them want him in a band, but by the time they see him, they’re like, he’s too little . . . his guitar is taller than him!” But Adrian is clear that music will be in his future. He said: “My dream would be to be the best guitarist in the world and be playing with famous bands and having fun with them too.” But playing the guitar has other benefits too. He added: “I usually just like it because it sounds good, it comes down my stress and it helps me play it and it helps me to just enjoy relax and play some good songs because usually most of the songs are heavy metal.” By sharing his journey on Instagram, Adrian and Abraham want to inspire others to do the same. Abraham said: “Like Adrian, you don’t have to wait to pick up a guitar. You can do it anytime, and you can’t, if Adrian can do it, so can you.” He joked: “I’ve got a daughter as well now she she’s only four years old, but she’s picked up the guitar because she thinks that’s the only way to get attention in the house!” Adrian and his dad, Abraham. articles.title: Rochdale Council plans major investments and heritage restoration
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council has announced significant investments in heritage restoration and community services, including plans for Hopwood Hall and Middleton's regeneration projects, aimed at boosting local economy and services.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has outlined a series of major investments aimed at revitalising the borough, with a focus on heritage restoration and community services. In a recent column, Councillor Neil Emmott highlighted the council's commitment to enhancing local infrastructure and supporting residents amid ongoing cost-of-living challenges.

A key development is the council's recent victory in the High Court regarding Hopwood Hall, a historic building in Middleton. The ruling provides clarity on the future of the site, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. Plans for essential repairs and feasibility studies are underway, with the aim of restoring the hall to serve the community and preserve its historical significance.

In addition to Hopwood Hall, the council is advancing its regeneration plans for Middleton. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to attract a new tenant by the end of the year, while the long-derelict Warwick Mill is also set for redevelopment, potentially including new housing. Furthermore, the transformation of the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue is in progress, aimed at providing activities and training for young people.

These initiatives are part of a broader strategy to stimulate economic growth and create jobs across the borough. With banking and post office services returning to Middleton town centre in the new year, local leaders are optimistic about the positive impact these developments will have on the community.

articles.title: Volunteers and council team tackle overgrown areas at Middleton’s Jubilee Park
articles.excerpt: The Friends of Jubilee Park and council staff have joined forces for the second phase of work to manage overgrown shrubs and care for the park’s rhododendrons.
articles.content_html:
Work to open up overgrown shrub areas at Jubilee Park in Middleton has entered its second phase, with volunteers and council staff joining forces to improve the grounds.

The Friends of Jubilee Park have been working alongside Rochdale Borough Council’s Environmental Management team, carrying out maintenance that includes caring for the park’s collection of rhododendrons.

The group says the work will encourage healthy new growth over the next couple of seasons, improve views and sight lines, and help visitors feel safer.

Opening up densely planted areas is intended to create a brighter, more welcoming park while supporting the long-term health of its shrubs.

Visitors may notice that some sections look temporarily untidy as the work progresses. The Friends have asked for patience, explaining that the maintenance is intended to bring lasting improvements.

“These improvements will bring lasting benefits for visitors and help Jubilee Park continue to thrive,” the group said.

The Friends describe Jubilee Park as a Gold Medal-winning Green Flag park and thanked visitors for their understanding while volunteers and staff care for the grounds.

The latest work forms part of an ongoing effort to maintain the much-loved Middleton green space for everyone who uses it.

articles.title: East Middleton councillor questions parking charge warning after petrol station breakdown
articles.excerpt: Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned about a parking charge while waiting for the RAC after her car broke down on Oldham Road.
articles.content_html:
Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned she could face a parking charge while waiting for recovery after her car broke down at a petrol station on Oldham Road.

Councillor Jacques, who represents East Middleton on Rochdale Borough Council, described the incident in a public Facebook post, asking whether the business could charge her when her vehicle would not start.

Writing about the breakdown, she said:

“So I’ve broken down in Petrol station on Oldham Road.

“Yes another car that’s absolutely useless ”

She then described a conversation with a member of staff:

“Anyway the guy working there said, I am gunna get charged for parking when his boss comes, as hes saying I can’t stay waiting for RAC!!! I can’t move my car obviously as it won’t start ”

According to her account, the vehicle was beside the station’s tyre inflation equipment. She wrote:

“it’s at the tyre pumper upper so not really blocking anywhere.

“So is this legal does anyone know surly they can’t charge me for breaking down.”

Councillor Jacques said the RAC had given her an estimated arrival window between 9.30pm and 11.30pm.

The screenshot does not establish that a parking charge was subsequently issued, how much was allegedly proposed, or which parking conditions applied. The petrol station is not named in the post, and its account of the conversation is not available.

Could she actually be charged?

A private parking operator can issue a parking charge where it alleges that a driver breached the site’s parking conditions. That is a civil payment demand, rather than a criminal charge. Whether a demand would be enforceable in this particular case cannot be determined from the Facebook post alone. The signage, terms, circumstances of the breakdown and evidence of the recovery arrangements would matter.

However, a breakdown gives a motorist a strong reason to challenge a ticket issued while waiting for repairs or recovery. Citizens Advice specifically identifies being unable to move a broken-down vehicle as grounds for an appeal. That does not guarantee automatic cancellation, but it means a demand should not simply be assumed valid.

Independent parking appeals service POPLA also identifies evidence of a breakdown and a recovery callout as relevant when exceptional circumstances prevented a driver from complying with parking conditions.

Drivers in this situation should retain recovery booking messages, attendance records and photographs of the parking signs. The Competition and Markets Authority advises motorists to preserve evidence when a breakdown occurs and to challenge a disputed charge rather than ignore it.

For now, Councillor Jacques’s post establishes that she reported being warned about a possible charge. It does not establish that she received one or that any payment was legally owed.

We hope Councillor Jacques is rescued promptly and back to her council duties in the morning—with her car feeling rather more cooperative.

articles.title: Teenager jailed for fatal crash in Middleton after teaching himself to drive
articles.excerpt: An 18-year-old has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison after causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly.
articles.content_html:
A teenager has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison for causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly. Ruhul Islam, now 18, taught himself to drive by watching YouTube videos and was behind the wheel of his brother's Nissan Micra when he struck Terence James, 78, on Shawbury Street on September 29, 2024.

During a hearing at Manchester Crown Court on October 13, it was revealed that Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries for a local business. Witnesses reported seeing him swerving through traffic, running red lights, and driving aggressively shortly before the crash. Mr James was crossing the road with his 10-year-old granddaughter when he was hit, suffering severe injuries that led to his death the following day after life support was withdrawn.

Judge Kate Cornell described the vehicle as a 'dangerous weapon' in the hands of someone unqualified to drive. She stated that Mr James would likely still be alive had Islam adhered to traffic laws. The court heard that Islam initially attempted to conceal his involvement in the crash, claiming his older brother was driving at the time.

The incident has raised concerns about road safety and the consequences of unlicensed driving. Following the sentencing, it is expected that discussions around stricter enforcement of driving regulations may take place, although no specific measures have been announced yet.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Unlicensed teen taught himself to drive on YouTube, ran red lights, then killed beloved dad in Middleton horror crash - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news Unlicensed teen taught himself to drive on YouTube, ran red lights, then killed beloved dad in Middleton horror crash Ruhul Islam was sentenced to six years and 11 months in prison following the death of Terence James View 4 Images Ruhul Islam had manipulated his brother into allowing him to use his car when Terence James was killed Add to preferred sources News Bethan Finighan Science and Innovation Writer 17:13, 14 Oct 2026 Updated 22:36, 14 Oct 2026 An unlicensed teenager who taught himself to drive by watching YouTube videos swerved through traffic and ran red lights before ploughing his older brother's Nissan Micra into a granddad who was crossing the road with his 10-year-old granddaughter. Terence James , 78, died after being struck by the vehicle on Shawbury Street, Middleton , on September 29, 2024. Yesterday (October 13), Manchester Crown Court heard how Ruhul Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries at the time of the offence. The 16-year-old was seen overtaking and undertaking vehicles, running red lights and weaving between lanes in the moments before the crash. Click here to hear the latest from Manchester's courts in our newsletter ‌ Now 18, he has been jailed for nearly seven years. Passing sentence, Judge Kate Cornell said: "The vehicle essentially became a dangerous weapon in the hands of someone unable to use it." View 4 Images Terence Lewis James, 78, who died after being struck by a car in Middleton (Image: Family submit) She said Mr James would still be alive had Islam driven on the correct side of the road, telling him: "That momentary lapse of judgement caused the tragedy that everyone in this room has to deal with for the rest of their lives… None of them will ever be the same again." The court heard Islam initially tried to hide that he had been driving and instead said his older brother was behind the wheel. Investigators later found Islam and his 16-year-old friend had been making deliveries for Chilli Pot takeaway in Middleton - a business owned by family friends - at the time of the offence. ‌ Shortly after 7pm, Islam turned right from Grimshaw Lane into Shawbury Street in Middleton and struck Mr James as he crossed the road. He was on the right carriageway of the road when he was hit, having already crossed the left carriageway. Prosecuting, Philip Hall told the court Islam "cut the corner by a significant margin". Mr James suffered a serious head injury and was rushed to Salford Royal hospital, where his condition deteriorated and he never regained consciousness. His family made the heartbreaking decision to withdraw life support the following evening. A witness who was in a nearby car park on Shawbury Street heard the collision and saw Mr James lying in the road. She gave him first aid and said she was 'surprised the two Asian males were not helping', prosecutors told the court. ‌ Another witness, the court heard, saw two men get out of the Nissan Micra before running away from the car. He said one man later emerged from the nearby takeaway and repeatedly insisted his brother had been driving and was only travelling at 10mph. The court was shown dashcam footage from the vehicle in the hour before the collision, which showed the car swerving between lanes in wet weather , "aggressive" overtaking and undertaking and driving through red lights. View 4 Images Ruhul Islam has been jailed for nearly seven years (Image: Greater Manchester Police) Four minutes before striking Mr James, footage showed Islam overtaking a vehicle into the opposing lane, before undertaking into a cycle lane. Two minutes before the collision, the vehicle made another "completely unnecessary" manoeuvre by contravening a traffic island on the other side of the road, the court heard. ‌ Islam initially failed to come forward as the driver after the fatal collision, with his older brother putting himself forward instead. After an investigation established Islam had been behind the wheel, both brothers were arrested at their home in Chadderton on November 24, 2024. In part of a police interview read to the court, Islam admitted teaching himself to drive by watching videos on YouTube and manipulating his brother, who has autism, to get the keys to his car. In her final remarks, Judge Cornell said: "You now accept that you manipulated and misled him to get his keys. You told him not to tell anyone." ‌ Judge Cornell also questioned how the adults in Islam's life "turned a blind eye" to his driving without a license, given he was just 16 years old and working for a family friend's business. View 4 Images Terence James, 78 (Image: Family submit) Defending, Michael Avery said Islam had no previous convictions or cautions and had received 11 positive character references, including one from Oldham Council Labour councillor Mohon Ali. He said the offence has had a "genuine impact on him and those closest to him", leaving Islam "withdrawn" and "spending more time in his room". The defence also referred to the impact of the offence on his mental health. ‌ Judge Cornell later said she accepted Islam's remorse was genuine and that he had experienced flashbacks and nightmares following the collision. In emotional statements read to the court, Mr James' grandson Harry James described him as a "soft and kind" man who was the "glue of the family". Caroline, one of Mr James's four children, described her father as the "kindest person I knew", saying he "would do anything for anyone and wouldn't hurt a fly". Describing the aftermath of the collision, Caroline rushed to the scene after her daughter, Daisy, returned to the house "hysterical", shouting that "grandad had been knocked down". ‌ She wrote in her statement that she saw her father on the ground as a woman put him in the recovery position. She said a man came out of the takeaway and apologised for what had happened. When she asked if he had been driving, she said he told her: "No, my brother, he's got autism". Addressing Islam, she wrote: "I have never been able to get over how the person in the dock lied to me. You didn't call an ambulance. You could see how upset I was and still came over and lied to my face…But you still tried to blame your brother." Islam pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving after initially pleading not guilty. He also pleaded guilty to causing death while unlicensed and uninsured and perverting the course of justice. ‌ Sentencing, Judge Cornell said Mr James had been "suddenly and heartbreakingly taken from his family". She said Islam's driving had been "clearly unrestrained by the rules of the road that we all have to follow and of course you never properly learned". The judge said there had been an element of "excitement and showing off" in his driving, with footage showing him overtaking and undertaking vehicles, driving in hatched areas and cycle lanes, and twice going through red lights. "Had you driven on the correct side of the road you would not have caused his death and he would be alive today," Judge Cornell said, adding that it was "only good fortune" that Mr James's granddaughter was not also hit or injured. Ruhul Islam, of Little Cot Close, Chadderton, was sentenced to six years and 11 months. He has also been disqualified from driving for eight years after his release. articles.title: Rochdale Council announces new regeneration projects for Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has unveiled a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, including the restoration of Hopwood Hall and the acquisition of Warwick Mill.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, following a recent High Court judgement in favour of the council regarding Hopwood Hall. This decision brings clarity to the future of the historic building, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. The council is committed to funding essential repairs and considering options for its long-term future.

In addition to the Hopwood Hall project, the council has made significant strides in Middleton's regeneration ambitions. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to lead to the announcement of a new tenant before the end of the year. Furthermore, the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be redeveloped for new housing, enhancing the local community.

Plans are also underway to transform the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue that will provide activities and training opportunities for young people. The council has also confirmed that banking and post office services will return to Middleton town centre in the new year, a move that is anticipated to provide a boost to the local economy.

These initiatives are part of the council's broader commitment to invest in the borough, creating jobs and driving economic growth. The council has also approved a £15 million support package over the next three years to assist residents facing financial difficulties, ensuring that help is available for those in need.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Borough means business as council delivers more pioneering projects | Rochdale Borough Council Search Search View menu Accessibility and translate Borough means business as council delivers more pioneering projects Left to right: Rose Marley and Steve Coogan, with Rochdale Borough Council Leader, Councillor Neil Emmott announcing new Middleton regeneration projects. It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. I want to begin with Hopwood Hall. The council welcomed the recent High Court judgement, which found in our favour and brings much-needed clarity about the future of this important historic building. While it's disappointing that a lengthy and potentially costly legal process was necessary, we are now focused on moving forward. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. I'm delighted that Middleton Old Grammar School, recently acquired by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. This follows news that the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be brought back into productive use, including the potential development of new homes. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. At the recent 'Our Town, Our Future' event, I saw first-hand the passion local residents, businesses and community groups have for Middleton and their determination to shape its future. It is an exciting time for the town, and we are turning ambition into action. Supporting residents through the cost-of-living crisis also remains a key priority. I am proud of the help we have provided through our Helping Hand campaign, which has supported thousands of older and vulnerable residents since 2022. As global economic pressures continue to affect household finances, the council has recently approved a further package of support worth around £15 million over the next three years through the Government's Crisis and Resilience Fund. This will provide emergency financial assistance, help residents keep their homes warm, debt and welfare advice, housing support, access to food provision and free warm spaces. We are committed to standing alongside residents who need support. This package will help reduce inequalities, ease pressure on household budgets and ensure thousands of people receive practical assistance throughout the autumn and winter months. My message is simple: if you need help, please get in touch. Further information is available at www.rochdale.gov.uk/costofliving or by calling 01706 923 685 . Finally, I want to highlight two important events that reflect our borough's strong and enduring support for the Armed Forces community. On Friday 16 October, Rochdale Town Hall will host a Festival of Remembrance featuring military music, marching bands, speeches, reflections and the Act of Remembrance. It promises to be a special evening and everyone is welcome to attend. Then, on Sunday 8 November, communities across the borough will come together for Remembrance Sunday services. It is always a poignant occasion, giving us the opportunity to honour and remember those who made the ultimate sacrifice in service of our country. For details of remembrance events across the borough, visit www.rochdale.gov.uk/events . Lest we forget. The council’s June 2026 update records construction. School places, healthcare capacity, drainage and transport obligations were not established from the material reviewed. Marketing claims about connectivity are useful context rather than an independent infrastructure assessment.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding against Duchy was established. That does not certify the company’s entire legal history or replace scrutiny of warranties and aftercare.

The development contributes to the borough’s housing supply through actual completions. Its full 56 homes should not be treated as still outstanding if some are already occupied.

A specific Rochdale housebuilder and site-specific adverse legal finding have not been verified here. The employment-led Northern Gateway and residential Simister/Bowlee programme should also be kept distinct when explaining approvals.

The core accountability question is whether cross-border delivery provides the services residents actually use, with an enforceable timetable rather than separate promises by different authorities.

The scheme could make a substantial contribution to housing supply over several years. Whether it meets local needs depends on who can afford the homes and how quickly the supporting services arrive.

articles.title: High Court rules against filmmaker in Hopwood Hall restoration dispute
articles.excerpt: A recent High Court ruling has concluded a legal battle between American filmmaker Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council over the future of Hopwood Hall in Middleton.
articles.content_html:
A High Court ruling has determined that American filmmaker Hopwood DePree does not have the right to purchase Hopwood Hall, a Grade-II* listed building in Middleton, following a protracted legal dispute with Rochdale Council. The decision was announced during a hearing at the Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, marking a significant setback for DePree, who has invested over £750,000 in efforts to restore the historic estate.

The saga began in 2017 when DePree signed an options agreement with the council to lead the redevelopment of Hopwood Hall. His vision included transforming the 1400s stately home into a wedding and hospitality venue, complete with a hotel retreat, gift shop, and guided tours. DePree engaged the local community in his restoration efforts, which included extensive work on the hall's gardens and interior.

Before DePree's involvement, Hopwood Hall had fallen into disrepair, with its last known use being as part of De La Salle College, which closed in 1989. The hall had previously served as a venue for various events, including an underground bar and nightclub during the 1960s and 70s, where notable acts such as Black Sabbath performed.

The ruling concludes a decade-long effort by DePree to revive the hall, which has been under the ownership of Rochdale Council since the college's closure. The future of Hopwood Hall now remains uncertain as the council considers its next steps regarding the estate.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The Hopwood Hall saga | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch The Hopwood Hall saga George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 10, 2026 | 8:44 AM Print The Grade-II listed Hopwood Hall in Middleton When an American filmmaker and Rochdale council signed an agreement over a shared ambition to restore Hopwood Hall, no one could have fathomed the furious saga that unfolded. What started as a harmonious relationship between Hopwood DePree and the local authority ended up with them being on opposite sides of a court room. Mr DePree claims ancestral connections to the Grade-II* listed building in Middleton. His dream was to bring the 1400s stately home back to life. He even roped in the local community to help him do it, apparently spending more than £750,000 on the project. On what he described as a ‘sad day’ in Manchester Civil Justice Centre last week, his dream was crushed. The High Court ruled in favour of the council following a legal battle over whether Mr DePree had the right to buy the estate or not. The saga began in 2017 when Hopwood DePree signed an options agreement with town hall bosses to lead the redevelopment of the hall. Since then he has led a decade-long community effort to do exactly that. The Hollywood man’s vision saw the hall transformed into a wedding and hospitality venue, with a hotel ‘retreat’, gift shop and guided tours all part of the package. His team could regularly be seen working on the hall’s gardens and titivating the interior in the years since. Before Mr DePree came along, the hall had fallen into disrepair and irrelevance. Its last known use was as part of the De La Salle College, which shut down in 1989. During the 1960s and 70s it was said to be the setting for an underground bar and nightclub. It is believed that Ozzy Osbourne’s band Black Sabbath and other iconic performers played there. Since the closure of the college, the hall has been in the possession of Rochdale council. The American even created a Youtube series and wrote a book about his journey refurbishing what he affectionately called ‘Downton Shabby’. However, this journey came to an abrupt halt when the council ended the agreement in October 2024 and, without warning, barred Mr DePree and his group from the building. Part of the options agreement allowed the US actor and producer to purchase the historic asset from landowners Rochdale council for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. Mr DePree attempted to exercise that option the day before the council ended the agreement, which was denied by town hall chiefs. Since then, a two-year-long war of words has raged between Mr DePree and Rochdale council. The American threatened legal action for months, but the council never budged. Mr DePree believed the local authority acted unlawfully by denying his ‘legally binding’ option to buy Hopwood Hall. At the time, the council said they ended the agreement because Mr DePree hadn’t made enough progress with the restoration effort. This expulsion from the estate came following a number of extensions to the agreement made by the council. The local authority even granted ‘change of use’ planning permission to Mr DePree for Hopwood Hall in 2022. Until the two sides decided to settle the matter in High Court, it was unclear just how important that planning permission was. Effectively, approved planning permission was the trigger to open up the option for Mr DePree to have the estate transferred to him. The High Court played host to Hopwood Hall Estate Ltd vs Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council this week. In the words of Mr DePree’s barrister, Ashley Bowes, the planning permission was ‘the star of the show’. The court heard details of the dispute over whether Mr DePree had authority to trigger the transfer of the property based on the approved plans. The council’s barrister Geraint Wheatley said the plans did not go far enough in demonstrating a serious commitment to reinstate and refurbish the 1400s building, as required by the options agreement. He described the ‘ruined’ hall as needing far more than some internal works to bring it back to a state of habitation. According to Mr Wheatley the conditions of the options agreement to trigger the purchase of the hall had four elements – authorisation to reinstate and refurbish the building; agreed standard of refurbishment between the parties (fit for habitation); English Heritage approval; and that the property would be reinstated and refurbished in whole, not in part. The defence barrister pointed out that getting permission for events and hospitality space for part of the ground floor doesn’t relate to the building ‘in whole’, as requested in the agreement clause. He also pointed out that the plans wouldn’t have seen the hall be fit for habitation or reinstated and refurbished. “Obtaining a mere ‘change of use’ permission doesn’t show a great deal of commitment,” Mr Wheatley told the court. “Plans of physical work show that commitment.” Mr Wheatley also tried to argue that English Heritage approval wasn’t given. But His Honour Judge Hodge KC believed the organisation’s support for the 2022 plans qualified as their approval. Buoyed by the judge agreeing with one point of the claimant, Dr Bowes said the 2022 application was internal work that would have created an events and hospitality space and enabled future work to be reinstated and refurbished. He said the claimant didn’t think anything more than a change of use application would be necessary to trigger the purchase as it wasn’t specified in the agreement. Dr Bowes said it was ‘wishful thinking’ on the council’s part that a community group would spend huge sums of money drawing up plans for physical works when they didn’t think it would be necessary. After delving into detailed planning legislation; the interpretation of wording in the agreement; and the cross-examinations of both Hopwood DePree and council boss for economy and place, Mark Robinson, the judge ruled in favour of the defendant – Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council. His Honour Judge Hodge KC described how the planning application did not cover the whole of the property or showcase the ability to reinstate and refurbish Hopwood Hall, as required in the options agreement. He added: “I am satisfied, for the reasons I have given, that the planning permission does not satisfy the requirements of the options agreement. I therefore refuse to grant the relief sought by the claimant.” A lengthy saga was ended by a two-day trial. Instead of getting Hopwood Hall for £1, Mr DePree was landed with a £114,000 bill to cover the council’s court costs. However, the American said the fight isn’t over and Hopwood Hall ‘must be saved’. He didn’t confirm whether his team would appeal the judgement, but they have until November 18 to do so. Speaking after the case, Mr DePree said: “Obviously I am incredibly disappointed. Not just me but the community of support around the world and the UK charitable groups as well. “I am already discussing with my legal team about the next steps. In the meantime I hope Rochdale council will be watching over Hopwood Hall because we will be keeping an eye on them. “We are not giving up. Hopwood Hall must be saved. In the two years we have been locked out the gardens have gone into wrack and ruin. I hope they will step up and save the hall. I still think the community group and I are the best people to take this forward. “I am getting messages from around the world with people offering money and support. It is a sad day but we will have to have a look at our options.” The town hall has committed to maintaining the building and have commissioned a feasibility study to look into possible future uses for the historic asset. A Rochdale council spokesperson said: “We are pleased with today’s judgement. It’s a shame that we had to endure a costly court battle to get to this point, as the time and money invested into this process could have been better spent on the hall itself. “We’re now focussed on moving forward. More than £1.6m has been spent on the hall by ourselves and Historic England since 2017 and we will continue to invest in vital repairs to this historic building. Feasibility studies have already been completed and options for Hopwood Hall’s long-term future will be considered in due course. “One thing we are clear on is, whatever the future holds for Hopwood Hall, this building, once restored and refurbished, will be used for the benefit of the wider community of Middleton who rightly cherish it as an important part of Middleton’s rich and varied heritage.” Add Roch Valley Radio as a preferred source on Google News to see more of our local reporting Add as a preferred source on Google Do you have a story for us? articles.title: £12m plan aims to bring Storage World Middleton site back to life after devastating fire
articles.excerpt: A £12m rebirth bid has been launched for the Storage World site in Middleton, more than a year after a devastating fire destroyed the Old Hall Street facility.
articles.content_html:
A £12m bid to bring the Storage World site in Middleton back to life has been launched, marking a major potential investment in an important part of the town centre following last year's devastating fire.

The proposals concern the Storage World site on Old Hall Street, next to Middleton Arena. The former storage facility was badly damaged by a major blaze in June 2025, which burned for several days and led to demolition of the building. No injuries were reported, although customers and businesses suffered significant losses.

Place North West has reported that Storage World has now launched a £12m rebirth bid for the site. The move comes as regeneration work and planning for the wider Middleton town centre area continues.

Official Rochdale Development Agency updates show that the council and RDA have remained in discussions with Storage World since the fire. In June, the RDA said it was working with stakeholders to develop key principles for the area, including the potential to deliver improvements to Middleton Arena and create a new public space. It also confirmed that discussions with Storage World were continuing with input from Rochdale Borough Council's planning team.

The site is particularly significant because of its position beside Middleton Arena and within an area being considered as part of wider plans for the future of Middleton town centre. Earlier council reports said the outcomes of discussions over Storage World and the arena would feed into wider masterplanning work.

Before the fire, Storage World operated a large self-storage and workspace facility from Old Hall Street. The Middleton operation had previously expanded as demand grew, with the company providing traditional storage alongside space used by small and online businesses.

The 2025 blaze had a substantial impact on customers. Fire crews worked for days at the scene and parts of the building were demolished while firefighting operations were still under way to allow crews safe access. Storage World said at the time that its team was devastated by the impact on customers and the wider community.

The latest £12m proposal therefore represents a potentially significant next chapter for a prominent town-centre site and comes at a time when Middleton is the subject of wider regeneration and masterplanning proposals.

Rochdale Daily will update this story as further planning documents and details of the proposed redevelopment become publicly available.

articles.title: Middleton protest planned as organiser sets out bail conditions ahead of event
articles.excerpt: A protest is planned in Middleton Gardens on 8 August, with organiser Jamie Thomason outlining his intended arrangements and referring to bail conditions while police are expected to oversee the event.
articles.content_html:
A public protest is due to take place in Middleton Gardens on Saturday, 8 August, with organiser Jamie Thomason stating he intends to comply with his bail conditions while addressing supporters before leaving the area. According to a statement published on social media, Greater Manchester Police will have officers present during the event, with police liaison officers said to be aware of the arrangements.

In his announcement, Thomason said he would be joined by several guest speakers from across the UK, including Ashlea Simon of All for England, Dorothy Jones and Pag Billy UK, with additional speakers yet to be confirmed. He described his planned speech as being based on information which he says can be verified through publicly available sources and encouraged supporters to attend the demonstration.

Thomason also referred to his current bail conditions, stating that he is prohibited from congregating with more than ten people. He asked supporters not to approach him in groups, saying he had agreed with Greater Manchester Police that he would attend, deliver his speech and leave Middleton immediately afterwards. He also stated that he would give his speech from a distance and would not become involved in any confrontation because he did not intend to breach his bail conditions.

Rochdale Daily has not independently verified the specific bail conditions referred to in Thomason's post, and reports them only as claims made by the organiser himself.

The right to peaceful protest is protected in UK law under Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, although that right is subject to restrictions where they are lawful, necessary and proportionate. Police have powers under the Public Order Act 1986, as amended by more recent legislation including the Public Order Act 2023, to impose conditions on public assemblies where they reasonably believe serious public disorder, serious disruption, intimidation or damage may occur. Participants are expected to comply with any lawful conditions imposed.

Greater Manchester Police has previously stated that its role at public demonstrations is to facilitate peaceful and lawful protest while taking action where criminal offences are committed or where public safety is at risk. Depending on the circumstances, officers may deploy protest liaison teams, public order officers or other resources to manage events and minimise disruption to the wider community.

The planned demonstration is likely to attract differing opinions from residents. Supporters say the event is intended to raise awareness of issues they believe are affecting communities across the country, while others are expected to disagree with both the organisers and the views expressed. Peaceful disagreement and lawful protest are protected rights, provided they remain within the limits of the law.

Anyone travelling through Middleton town centre on Saturday should be aware that there may be an increased police presence around Middleton Gardens while the demonstration takes place. At the time of publication, no official road closures, dispersal orders or protest conditions had been publicly announced.

Rochdale Daily has contacted Greater Manchester Police for comment to confirm the policing arrangements for the event, including whether officers will be deployed, whether any conditions have been imposed under public order legislation, and whether any road closures, dispersal powers or other measures are anticipated. This article will be updated if and when a response is received.
